text: Joining me now for more on the historic
midterm elections for Democrats is New
York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani who
endorsed a number of Democratic
candidates throughout this midterm
cycle. Mayor, thank you so much for
joining me. So, what's your reaction to
last night's results?
>> It was an incredible evening and I think
what it showed is that the American
people are tired of being told that
their needs are unrealistic by the very
politicians that have been bought off by
the wealthiest people in the country.
And you know, we heard from J.D. Vance
asking Americans across the country for
2 more years and what those same
Americans have said in response is they
can't afford to wait 2 more years when
their rent is due on the first of the
month, when they have to pay for their
groceries today, when they have to get
their kids to child care this week.
>> Well, let me ask you because with the
exception of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan,
nearly all of the Democrats' biggest
statewide victories were more moderate
candidates. What do you think that says
and what does it say about the
progressive movement?
>> Well, I want to push you a little bit on
that, Kristen, because when we're
thinking about James Talarico, we're
talking about somebody who campaigned on
universal pre-K. When we're talking
about Annie Andrews, we're talking about
somebody who campaigned on an end to
endless wars. When we're talking about
Keisha Lance Bottoms, we're talking
about somebody who campaigned on
streamlining the construction of
affordable housing and those are all the
hallmarks of what progressive governance
also looks like in this country and I
think it's critically important that
when we look at these victories, no
matter where they are across the United
States, that we understand the unity of
purpose that comes out of it and the
urgency of delivering change that
Americans can feel in their wallets.
>> So, Mayor, given this argument that
you're making, do you think there is a
path for a progressive candidate in the
presidential race in 2028?
>> Absolutely.
>> And why? What gives you that confidence?
>> We we have heard time and again over the
10 months that I've been in office here
in New York City that what we're doing
here can't work elsewhere. That what
people are concerned about here isn't
what people are concerned about across
the country. And what we saw last night
is that the struggles of Americans in
Atlanta, of Americans in Allentown, are
not all that different than the
struggles of Americans in Astoria. And
that is a reflection of the fact that
dignity has to be at the heart of our
politics and it has to be at the heart
of our vision for what comes next.
Because we've had the debate for a
number of years. Now is the time for us
in the Democratic Party to deliver. And
we have to deliver with the same urgency
that Americans have given us this
mandate.
>> Well, what is the mandate do you think
that Democrats have given that voters
have given to Democrats?
>> I see it as a mandate to deliver on the
cost of living crisis that has affected
Americans across this country. A mandate
to build schools not bombs. A mandate to
actually fulfill the trust that has been
given to us by working-class voters. And
that to me is a mandate that understands
that politics cannot simply be about
better managing the decline of our
country. It has to be about inspiring
our country to reach heights that we've
never seen before. And that comes from a
recognition of the fact that what makes
this the greatest country in the world
is the working-class people who build it
every single day.
>> As you know, there's a big debate right
now inside the Democratic Party about
how far to go when it comes to
oversight, investigations, and there's a
lot of discussion about potentially
impeaching President Trump for a third
time. Is that something that you would
support understanding that you're not in
the Congress, but is that something that
ideologically and and strategically you
would support?
>> I would support our Congress taking
action that will deliver change in
Americans' lives that they can feel in
their wallets. And I would also support
our Congress taking action to confront
the corruption that we have seen in
Washington for far too long. Americans
have been voting for a new vision of
government and it's time that we hear
that and don't try and confine it into
just one lane of what that politics must
mean. I believe in so many of the people
elected last night's ability to take
action across the board.
>> Do you think it could backfire though if
Democrats do move to impeach President
Trump?
>> That's not something that I've heard as
as a plan right now from from those who
have been speaking up over the last 24
hours. What I have heard time and again
is how we can move with the urgency of
action that's been required by the
American people. And to me, it is an
urgency that speaks about data centers,
it's an urgency that speaks about
tariffs, it's an urgency that speaks
about the fact that we have continued to
fund the violation of international law
across so many parts of the world when
especially when we're looking at
Palestine and even when we're looking at
Iran. And that is something that needs
to be confronted and I'm excited at the
fact that we now have the opportunity to
do so.
>> Well, in order for this Democratic
Congress to deliver results, they're
going to have to work with President
Trump because he does have veto power.
He's made it very clear he's not afraid
to use it. You're someone who has worked
with President Trump. You've gone to the
Oval Office. What is your advice to your
fellow Democrats about how they can get
things done in Washington?
>> What what I found has been the most
productive approach to this relationship
has been the fact that both the
President and I are very open and honest
about the immense number of policy
disagreements that we have and amidst
that looking for any place of
commonality. And when it comes to the
two of us, that commonality has been the
welfare of our city. We've had
conversations that have allowed us to
free New Yorkers from ICE detention, to
ensure that we were able to get a visa
for the mother of a New Yorker who was
killed here recently. These are the
kinds of tangible benefits that can be
delivered when we're looking for any of
those areas of overlap. And I'm looking
forward to whatever opportunity there is
in working with whomever across whatever
party line to deliver for working people
across our city.
>> Do you think that Democrats should take
the possibility of a government shutdown
off the table? In other words, do you
think that's sort of the opposite of
what people voted for last night?
>> I think what people voted for last night
is an affirmative vision, and I think
what people voted for last night is an
urgency and an unwillingness to be told
to wait any longer. And you can see that
both in terms of the politics that
prevailed and also in terms of the
generational change, where we saw a
number of younger candidates also step
forward and say, "The time is now to
change this kind of a status quo." And
that is something that excites me. I
know there are a lot of these decisions,
you know, they're going to be in the
hands of Congress people and I trust
them to make the right ones. What I will
say as the mayor of New York City is
they're excited to have partners in the
fight to bring dignity back into working
people's lives.
>> Well, and speaking of one of the issues
that the Congress is going to address
and that your
fellow Democrats are going to address in
Washington is who is going to be their
next speaker of the House. You've said
you would support your fellow New Yorker
Hakeem Jeffries as speaker. You're not
going to have a vote though. Are you
going to encourage your fellow
Democrats in Washington to support him?
>> I'm going to leave the machinations of
that to my uh fellow Democrats in
Washington. I've been clear about where
I stand and I think that's all they need
to hear from me on that.
>> And what about Leader Schumer?
>> I think it's it's it's the same. There
are some decisions that I will leave to
to those in in Washington and I can just
be clear about where I stand as the
mayor of our city.
>> Do you think they both represent the
type of what they have described as
generational change that voters
delivered overnight?
>> I think it all comes from the vision
that we put forward. It's less about us
as individuals, it's more about the
agenda that we will now pursue. Because
power is not something that should just
be sought to be won. It's something that
should be used to actually deliver. And
that is what we have the opportunity to
do today. It is the dawning of a new day
and it's up to us to seize it.
>> Let me just ask you one more question.
It's been really notable. Vice President
J.D. Vance had a really long post today,
effectively blaming the war with Iran
for the election losses that Republicans
suffered. Do you think trying to end
this war should be at the top of
Democrats' agenda and how can they go
about that?
>> Yes. Yes, it should. It is a war that is
not only illegal, it is one that should
be opposed on political grounds, on
economic grounds, on moral grounds. And
it is something that the American people
have spoken up loud and clear about. And
I have to say that I find it quite
ironic to read a post from the vice
president as if he's describing the
actions of a different administration.
He's the vice president of the United
States of America. He is not just some
commentator online. And there has to be
a reckoning of the fact that this is a
war that they started. It's a war that
they can end. If they think it was a
part of their political demise, then why
don't they actually start to take some
action to reflect that?
>> All right. Well, Mayor Zoran Mamdani,
always appreciate our conversations.
Thanks so much for joining me on this
very busy day after election day.
>> Thank you so much for having me. Always
a pleasure.
